screens.title: Organizing and Executing BDD Tests
screens.subtitle: Project layout, hooks, tagging, reporting, and CI/CD integration for maintainable BDD automation

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn pragmatic ways to organize a BDD automation project and how to execute tests so they remain fast, reliable, and useful. We’ll walk through a clear project layout that separates feature files, step definitions, and support code, and we’ll explain Cucumber hooks for lifecycle setup and teardown so your tests start each scenario in a known state. You’ll see how tagging gives you selective runs for smoke and regression suites, what reports Cucumber can produce, and how to wire tests into a CI/CD pipeline so failures give immediate feedback. Along the way I’ll show concrete examples you can copy directly into your project and a typical mistake to avoid that causes flaky tests. By the end, you’ll understand how organization, hooks, tagging, and reporting work together to keep BDD suites maintainable and valuable as a team grows. Think of this chapter as the operational handbook that turns feature files into reliable, actionable verification.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Good structure and execution make BDD suites dependable. Proper hooks, tags, and reports let teams run focused tests and trust results in CI.

Organizing and Executing BDD Tests

Learn a practical project layout, lifecycle hooks, tagging strategies, and reporting so your suite stays fast and actionable.

Project Health
Structure, hooks, tags
Orientation

This chapter focuses on organization and execution: put feature files under src/test/resources/features, keep step definitions and support code in src/test/java with clear packages, use hooks for lifecycle control, apply tags to build targeted suites, collect machine- and human-friendly reports, and integrate execution into CI so tests validate every change.

Hooks

Coming up

We will first define a clean file layout, then examine hooks and tagging with code examples, look at reporting outputs, and finally demonstrate how to run BDD tests in CI pipelines.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you should be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to design a maintainable BDD project structure, add and scope Cucumber hooks for reliable setup and teardown, use tags to run focused test suites, and produce and interpret Cucumber reports. You’ll also understand basic strategies for plugging BDD runs into a CI/CD pipeline so tests validate each build. Each objective maps to a practical competence: organizing files prevents step-definition chaos; scoped hooks avoid slow or flaky runs; tagging keeps fast smoke and deep regression suites separate; and machine-friendly reports let your pipeline surface failures without guessing. For example, placing feature files in src/test/resources/features and step classes in src/test/java grouped by package immediately makes it easier to find code when a scenario breaks. A correctly scoped @Before hook creates the browser only once per scenario instead of per step, preventing excessive test duration. These abilities will let you maintain an executable specification that a team can trust and operate within automation pipelines.

keyIdea.title: Four practical outcomes
keyIdea.text: Organize, hook, tag, and report—then run from CI. Each step reduces maintenance cost and prevents flaky failures.

screens.title: Project Layout: Features, Steps, Support Code
screens.subtitle: A clear folder and package structure keeps BDD suites maintainable

narration.text: A stable BDD project starts with a predictable layout. Place Gherkin feature files under src/test/resources/features so tools discover them without extra configuration. Within that folder, group related features into subdirectories by functional area — for example, features/authentication and features/product_catalog. Step definitions belong in src/test/java under packages that mirror those areas, such as com. cohortia. steps. authentication and com. cohortia. steps. product. This parallel structure reduces the cognitive load when a scenario fails: you know where to look. Keep support code separate in packages like com. cohortia. pages for Page Objects, com. cohortia. api for A P I clients, and com. cohortia. utils for helpers. Support code handles the how of interactions while step definitions describe the what; this separation keeps step classes focused and small. A concrete example: a login feature file in features/authentication will have step methods in com. cohortia. steps. authentication and the page interactions in com. cohortia. pages. LoginPage. A common misconception is to mix utility methods into step classes — that causes duplication and harder refactoring. The key takeaway is to design folders and packages that map to your product domains and keep support code separate for easier maintenance.

keyIdea.title: Folder mapping
keyIdea.text: Mirror feature directories with step packages and keep support code in dedicated packages to separate intent from implementation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Project Layout
Definition

Organize features, steps, and support code

A modular layout places feature files under resources, step definitions in test Java packages, and support classes in dedicated packages. That separation keeps steps concise and reusable.

Feature folder
src/test/resources/features and subfolders per domain, e.g., features/authentication.
Step packages
src/test/java/com/cohortia/steps. keeps related step classes together.
Support code
com/cohortia/pages, com/cohortia/api, com/cohortia/utils — separate from glue code.
Concrete example
Example mapping
  • features/authentication/login.feature
  • src/test/java/com/cohortia/steps/authentication/LoginSteps.java
  • src/test/java/com/cohortia/pages/LoginPage.java
Common mistake
Putting page interactions directly in step classes — this makes steps large and hard to reuse. Keep step definitions declarative and delegate implementation to support classes.
Key Takeaway

Map features to step packages and keep support code separate so tests are readable and maintainable.

screens.title: Support Code: Page Objects, API Clients, Utilities
screens.subtitle: Why support code belongs outside step definitions

narration.text: Support code is auxiliary logic that handles how interactions with the system occur, leaving step definitions to describe behavior. Page Objects encapsulate UI interactions, exposing intent-focused methods like navigateToLogin or enterCredentials. A P I client classes wrap HTTP calls and response parsing so steps can say, for example, request user creation rather than craft raw requests inline. Utility classes centralize common helpers like test data builders, wait helpers, or serialization. By locating these classes in dedicated packages such as com. cohortia. pages, com. cohortia. api, and com. cohortia. utils, step definitions remain short and expressive. A concrete example is LoginSteps calling LoginPage. login(username, password) rather than locating elements and typing directly. A common misconception is that support code slows iteration because it adds indirection; in reality it speeds maintenance — when a selector changes you update the Page Object once. The practical rule: put implementation details in support code, keep step methods readable and close to the business language in the feature file. This keeps executable specifications valuable as living documentation. Support Code: Page Objects, API Clients, Utilities means support code handles implementation; step definitions express behavior. this makes both easier to maintain.. In practical terms, why support code belongs outside step definitions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Separation of concerns
keyIdea.text: Support code handles implementation; step definitions express behavior. This makes both easier to maintain.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Support Code
What is support code?

Page Objects, API clients, utilities

Support code encapsulates how interactions happen. Use Page Objects for UI actions, API clients for backend calls, and utilities for reuseable helpers.

Page Objects
Provide methods like login(), clickSubmit(), and getErrorMessage() so steps call intent-focused APIs.
API Clients
Wrap request and response handling so tests use high-level calls instead of raw HTTP.
Utilities
Centralize data builders, waits, and parsing helpers to avoid duplication across steps.
Concrete example
LoginSteps → LoginPage
LoginSteps calls LoginPage.login(username, password). LoginPage finds elements and performs typing and submit. If selectors change, update LoginPage only.
Misconception
Putting interaction details in step definitions makes steps harder to read and maintain. Delegate implementation to support code instead.
Key Takeaway

Keep step definitions declarative; let support code handle implementation details so fixes are centralized.

narration.text: Cucumber hooks let you run code at predictable points in the test lifecycle. Use @Before and @After for scenario-level setup and teardown — for example, initialize a WebDriver, set test data, or reset a database. These hooks run once per scenario and are the right place for heavier operations. @BeforeStep and @AfterStep execute around every step; reserve them for very lightweight tasks such as logging, metrics, or taking a small screenshot when a step fails. A common pitfall is placing expensive setup in @BeforeStep or @AfterStep — doing so will repeat the heavy work for every step and dramatically increase runtime. Hooks are normally placed in a dedicated Hooks class inside your glue package so they are easy to manage and reuse. Also, you can scope hooks to tags so some setup runs only for scenarios marked with a specific tag. The practical aim is to make each scenario independent: if @After reliably cleans up state, scenarios won’t leak state into one another. That predictability reduces flakiness and makes debugging straightforward. Cucumber Hooks and Lifecycle means use scenario-level hooks for heavy setup/teardown and step-level hooks only for lightweight operations to avoid slow suites.. In practical terms, when to use @before, @after, @beforestep, and @afterstep. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hook rules
keyIdea.text: Use scenario-level hooks for heavy setup/teardown and step-level hooks only for lightweight operations to avoid slow suites.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Cucumber Hooks
Lifecycle overview

When hooks run

@Before
Runs once before each scenario. Use it for initializing WebDriver, test data, or common mocks.
@After
Runs after each scenario regardless of outcome. Close resources and clean state here.
@BeforeStep / @AfterStep
Runs for every step. Keep these lightweight — logging or conditional screenshots only.
Best practice
Place all hooks in a Hooks.java or ScenarioHooks.java within your glue package so they are discovered by Cucumber and easy to maintain. Scope with tags when needed to avoid running unnecessary setup for unrelated scenarios.
Common mistake
Putting heavy setup in @BeforeStep/@AfterStep which executes per step and slows the suite dramatically.
Key Takeaway

Use scenario hooks for heavy operations and step hooks for minimal per-step tasks like logging.

screens.title: Hooks.java Example
screens.subtitle: A practical Hooks class with tag-scoped setup and teardown

narration.text: Let's walk through a typical Hooks. java implementation that demonstrates both general and tag-scoped hooks. The example uses @Before and @After to run logic for all scenarios and also shows tag-specific hooks that run only for scenarios annotated with a given tag. You will notice the class prints scenario names to the console and performs conditional actions like taking a screenshot on failure. In the real project, these print statements represent initialization of WebDriver, mocks, or database seeds. The key detail is that @Before runs once per scenario to create resources, while @After will always run to clean them. Tagged hooks limit scope so specialized setup for smoke tests does not run for every scenario. A common misconception is that multiple hooks conflict — they run in sequence and can be ordered, but keep them small and focused. Review the code example in the panel and imagine replacing system prints with real initialization and cleanup calls. This concrete pattern is safe and practical for most BDD Java projects. Hooks.java Example means use general hooks for all scenarios and tag-scoped hooks when only some scenarios need extra setup or cleanup.. In practical terms, a practical hooks class with tag-scoped setup and teardown. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hook pattern
keyIdea.text: Use general hooks for all scenarios and tag-scoped hooks when only some scenarios need extra setup or cleanup.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Hooks.java Example
Example code
// In com.cohortia.steps/Hooks.java
import io.cucumber.java.After;
import io.cucumber.java.Before;
import io.cucumber.java.Scenario;

public class Hooks {

    @Before
    public void setupScenario(Scenario scenario) {
        System.out.println("--- Starting scenario: " + scenario.getName() + " ---");
        // Initialize WebDriver, database connection, etc.
    }

    @After
    public void teardownScenario(Scenario scenario) {
        System.out.println("--- Finished scenario: " + scenario.getName() + " with status: " + scenario.getStatus() + " ---");
        // Close WebDriver, clean up database, etc.
    }
}
Explanation
  • @Before receives a Scenario instance so you can log or seed test data based on scenario name or tags.
  • @After runs even if a scenario fails; use it to close drivers and reset state to avoid leakage.
  • Replace prints with actual setup like driver initialization and teardown with driver.quit().
Misuse to avoid
Do not put heavy per-step logic in @BeforeStep. That will run for every step and slow tests severely.
Key Takeaway

Use scenario hooks to prepare and clean resources; keep them concise and tag-scoped when needed.

screens.title: Tagging Scenarios for Selective Execution
screens.subtitle: Use tags to build smoke, regression, and targeted suites without changing feature files

narration.text: Tagging is a simple but powerful mechanism built into Gherkin. Prefix features or scenarios with labels such as @SmokeTest, @Regression, or custom domain tags. Once tags exist, your TestRunner can include or exclude them with logical expressions. For example, tags = "@SmokeTest" runs only smoke tests, while tags = "@SmokeTest and @Regression" requires both tags. You can combine OR logic and negation like tags = "@SmokeTest or @LoginFeature" or tags = "not @NegativeTest" to exclude scenarios. This lets you maintain a single set of feature files while offering fast-running smoke suites and thorough regression suites. A common practical pattern is to tag quick verification scenarios with @SmokeTest and longer end-to-end flows with @Regression. To verify the behavior, tag the relevant scenarios in your feature files and then run mvn test with your TestRunner configured to the desired tag expression. A misconception is that tags change execution order; they only filter which scenarios run. Takeaway: tags are a stable way to compose suites without editing code during execution. Tagging Scenarios for Selective Execution means tags let you select scenarios at runtime using logical expressions so you can run fast or deep suites as needed.. In practical terms, use tags to build smoke, regression, and targeted suites without changing feature files. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Tagging power
keyIdea.text: Tags let you select scenarios at runtime using logical expressions so you can run fast or deep suites as needed.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Tagging Scenarios
Gherkin examples
@SmokeTest @LoginFeature
Feature: User Login

  @Regression
  Scenario: Successful login with valid credentials
    Given I have entered 5 into the calculator
    When I press the add button
    Then the result should be 12 on the screen

  @SmokeTest @NegativeTest
  Scenario: Failed login with invalid credentials
    # ... steps ...
Runner expressions
tags = "@SmokeTest" | tags = "@SmokeTest and @Regression" | tags = "not @NegativeTest"
Why use tags?
  • Create fast smoke suites for quick feedback.
  • Run deep regression suites on schedule or before release.
  • Exclude known-failing or long-running tests from daily runs.
Misunderstanding
Tags filter which scenarios execute; they do not change the scenario logic or ordering by themselves.
Key Takeaway

Tag scenarios to create focused suites and manage test runtime without changing feature content.

screens.title: TestRunner.java and Tag Configuration
screens.subtitle: Configure Cucumber options to include plugins and tag expressions

narration.text: The TestRunner ties together your features, glue code, plugins, and tags. In Java projects you typically create a TestRunner with @CucumberOptions specifying the features path, glue package, plugin outputs, and a tags expression. The chapter example configures pretty output for the console, an H T M L report for human consumption, and a JSON file for machine processing. Tags = "@SmokeTest" runs only scenarios annotated with that tag, which is ideal for quick validation in pre-merge checks. The JSON output is particularly useful because other reporting tools can read it to build dashboards. Remember that plugin outputs are file paths; include json:target/cucumber. json and junit:target/cucumber. xml if your CI expects those formats. A common misconception is that adding many plugins slows execution; plugin generation adds some IO but gives visibility that is often worth the cost. When running in CI, prefer machine-readable formats so pipeline tools can parse and display test results automatically. TestRunner.java and Tag Configuration means testrunner configures discovery, output, and tag filters so test runs can be tailored for local or ci environments.. In practical terms, configure cucumber options to include plugins and tag expressions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Runner responsibility
keyIdea.text: TestRunner configures discovery, output, and tag filters so test runs can be tailored for local or CI environments.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › TestRunner.java
Example
package com.cohortia.runners;

import io.cucumber.junit.Cucumber;
import io.cucumber.junit.CucumberOptions;
import org.junit.runner.RunWith;

@RunWith(Cucumber.class)
@CucumberOptions(
    features = "src/test/resources/features",
    glue = "com.cohortia.steps",
    plugin = {"pretty", "html:target/cucumber-reports.html", "json:target/cucumber.json"},
    tags = "@SmokeTest"
)
public class TestRunner {
}
Explanation
  • features: path where Cucumber looks for .feature files.
  • glue: package(s) containing step definitions and hooks.
  • plugin: defines human and machine report outputs such as html and json.
  • tags: expression to filter which scenarios run.
Practical tip
Use json output for downstream reporting tools and html for quick human inspection after a pipeline run.
Key Takeaway

Configure TestRunner to match your local and CI needs: discovery, plugins, and tags are its main responsibilities.

screens.title: Cucumber Reports: Console, HTML, JSON, JUnit
screens.subtitle: Pick the right outputs for humans and tools

narration.text: Reporting gives teams insight into what ran and why. Cucumber provides multiple built-in outputs. The pretty plugin is a human-friendly console log that is useful during local development. H T M L output creates a readable summary report for quick inspection after a run. JSON output is machine-readable and is commonly fed into external reporting tools to produce richer dashboards. JUnit XML is used by many CI systems to display test results directly in the pipeline UI. Choose a combination: pretty for local debugging, html for manual review, and json or junit for CI processing. For example, the TestRunner can include plugin = {"pretty", "html:target/cucumber-reports. html", "json:target/cucumber. json"}. A common misconception is that reports alone fix flaky tests — they help you find failures, but you still need proper hooks and cleanup to prevent flakiness. The practical rule is to generate both human and machine outputs so developers can read a failing scenario quickly while the pipeline captures standardized results for dashboards and gating decisions. Cucumber Reports: Console, HTML, JSON, JUnit means use console and html for human review, and json/junit for ci and tool integration to ensure visibility and automation.. In practical terms, pick the right outputs for humans and tools. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Report roles
keyIdea.text: Use console and HTML for human review, and JSON/JUnit for CI and tool integration to ensure visibility and automation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Cucumber Reports
Built-in plugins
pretty
Readable console output for quick inspection while developing.
html:target/cucumber-reports.html
Human-friendly HTML report saved to target for post-run review.
json:target/cucumber.json
Machine-readable output consumed by dashboard tools like Allure or ExtentReports.
Practical guidance
  • Produce both human and machine outputs for developer and pipeline needs.
  • Store reports as pipeline artifacts so they are available after runs.
  • Use JSON for downstream rich reporting tools and JUnit for CI test summaries.
Misconception
Reports show failures but won’t fix flaky tests by themselves. Use them to guide root-cause fixes.
Key Takeaway

Emit both human and machine reports so teams can triage locally and pipelines can gate releases automatically.

screens.title: Integrating BDD Runs into CI/CD
screens.subtitle: Trigger tests on build and use reports to gate deployments

narration.text: Integrating BDD into CI/CD creates a continuous validation loop: after code is built, tests run automatically and results determine whether a build advances. The typical pattern is to run mvn test or gradle test as a pipeline step, collect JUnit XML and JSON artifacts, and have the pipeline parse those artifacts to mark the build as passed, unstable, or failed. For quick feedback on pull requests, run a smoke tag expression such as @SmokeTest. For nightly or release jobs, run the full regression suite. CI servers like Jenkins, GitLab CI, GitHub Actions, and Azure DevOps can run the same commands and surface results directly in their dashboards. The key is to ensure test data and environment configuration are reproducible in CI; use environment variables, test containers, or mocks to isolate external dependencies. A common pitfall is relying on local developer resources in CI — that causes flaky pipeline runs. The practical takeaway is to design your pipeline stages to run targeted tests early and broader suites later, and to publish the H T M L or machine-readable reports so teams can review failures quickly.

keyIdea.title: CI pipeline pattern
keyIdea.text: Run smoke tests on PRs, full regression on scheduled builds, and publish machine-readable reports for pipeline gating and dashboards.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › CI/CD Integration
Pipeline stages
  1. Build and compile the project so tests run against current code.
  2. Run targeted tests (tags = "@SmokeTest") on pull requests for fast feedback.
  3. Run the full regression suite on scheduled or pre-release jobs.
  4. Collect reports and publish them as artifacts for triage.
Practical notes
Use environment variables for config, mock external services where possible, and ensure reproducible test data so pipeline runs are deterministic.
Common pitfalls
  • Relying on local-only services that are not available in CI.
  • Generating non-deterministic test data leading to flaky pipeline failures.
  • Not publishing reports, making failure triage slow.
Key Takeaway

Design CI stages to run fast checks early and deeper suites later, and publish machine-readable reports so the pipeline can gate releases.

screens.title: Preventing Flaky Tests and Common Mistakes
screens.subtitle: Avoid slow hooks, shared state leaks, and inconsistent cleanup

narration.text: Flaky tests erode trust in automation. Much of flakiness stems from inconsistent environment setup or leftover state between scenarios. Ensure @After hooks consistently clean browser instances, reset databases, and clear caches so each scenario begins with a known state. Avoid heavy work in @BeforeStep/@AfterStep because they run per step and dramatically increase execution time. Another root cause is dependence on external services that vary; use mocks or test doubles in CI or configure test data so responses are predictable. When debugging flakiness, examine reports for patterns: failures clustered around certain scenarios often point to shared state leakage. A practical mitigation is to isolate tests into smaller suites using tags, allowing you to reproduce failures quickly. A common misunderstanding is assuming adding retries hides flakiness; retries mask symptoms but not the underlying problem. Instead, invest in reliable setup and teardown, clear separation of support code, and small, focused tests that are easier to reason about. That approach reduces noise and keeps the automation suite trustworthy. Preventing Flaky Tests and Common Mistakes means consistent cleanup, minimal per-step work, and isolating dependencies are the main levers to reduce flaky tests.. In practical terms, avoid slow hooks, shared state leaks, and inconsistent cleanup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fix flakiness
keyIdea.text: Consistent cleanup, minimal per-step work, and isolating dependencies are the main levers to reduce flaky tests.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Flaky Tests & Mistakes
Common causes
  • Shared state between scenarios due to incomplete cleanup.
  • Heavy per-step hooks that slow and destabilize tests.
  • Dependency on external services without mocks in CI.
Don't do this
Open and close browsers in step hooks or rely on network services without a stable test fixture.
Practical fixes
  1. Use @Before/@After for resource lifecycle and ensure @After always resets state.
  2. Mock external dependencies or use stable test doubles in CI.
  3. Isolate flaky scenarios and reduce their scope until root cause is fixed.
Key Takeaway

Prevent flakiness by ensuring deterministic setup and teardown, minimizing per-step work, and isolating external dependencies in CI.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: These three cards summarize the essentials: support code keeps step definitions concise, hooks manage the lifecycle so scenarios are independent, and tags plus reports let you run and observe focused suites. Support code such as Page Objects and A P I clients encapsulate implementation details so a single change updates all steps. Hooks like @Before and @After are your place for heavier initialization and cleanup, while @BeforeStep and @AfterStep should be reserved for very lightweight tasks. Tagging enables fast smoke or targeted runs without changing feature files, and generating both human-readable and machine-readable reports ensures developers and pipelines can act on failures. Together these practices keep BDD suites maintainable and trustworthy. As you apply them, ask: can I find the feature, step, and supporting class quickly? Is my setup fast and deterministic? Do my reports provide actionable detail? If the answer is yes, your BDD automation is behaving as an executable specification and a reliable guardrail for your delivery pipeline.

keyIdea.title: Three pillars
keyIdea.text: Support code, lifecycle hooks, and tagging + reporting are the core practices for maintainable BDD automation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Key Concepts
Support Code
Encapsulates implementation so steps remain declarative.
Hooks
@Before/@After manage scenario lifecycle; use step hooks sparingly.
Tags & Reports
Tags select suites; reports provide human and CI-readable outputs.
Summary Takeaway

A structured project, scoped hooks, disciplined tagging, and both human and machine reports form the foundation of maintainable, trustworthy BDD automation.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Practical Reminders
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to guide your work

narration.text: Keep these three practical reminders at hand: first, mirror feature directories with step packages and keep support code in dedicated packages to make behavior easy to find and fix. Second, place heavy initialization and cleanup in @Before and @After hooks and reserve per-step hooks for trivial actions. Third, use tags to compose fast smoke suites for pull requests and schedule deeper regression runs, while generating both human and machine reports so teams and CI systems can act on failures. Each reminder reduces maintenance overhead and improves the reliability of your automation. Before you commit changes, ask whether the hooks are scoped correctly, if the support code belongs in a reusable class, and whether a tag exists so you can run this scenario quickly in isolation. These checks help prevent flaky tests and keep your BDD suite a dependable collaborator in the delivery process.

keyIdea.title: Practical checklist
keyIdea.text: Structure, scoped hooks, and tag-driven suites keep tests maintainable, fast, and actionable in CI.

Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Practical Reminders
Mirror structure
Features ↔ step packages; support code separate.
Scope hooks
@Before/@After for heavy work; step hooks for small tasks.
Tag & report
Use tags for selective runs and reports for CI visibility.
Final Thought

Small structural choices and disciplined execution habits prevent large maintenance costs later. Keep tests readable, deterministic, and observable.
